item.title: YC Labs and Olam Labs run multi-agent GPT-6.1 swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry to study emergent behaviors and coordination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: YC Labs partnered with Olam Labs to conduct experiments using swarms of 25 to 50 GPT-6.1 agents in Minecraft and Mindustry, aiming to understand multi-agent dynamics and AI alignment challenges. The agents were tasked with survival and civilization-building goals, exhibiting emergent behaviors such as role formation, hierarchy, and complex coordination. In Minecraft, 50 agents operated in a survival world for three hours, building shelters, managing resources, and establishing a pseudo-government with rules and rationing. The agents communicated extensively, adapted to environmental hazards, and developed risk-averse behaviors after early losses. The project involved creating an open-source agent harness to enable long-running, interactive AI agents in the game environment. These experiments provide empirical insights into how AI agent swarms coordinate and evolve strategies in open-world settings, informing both the potential benefits and risks of multi-agent AI systems.

item.title: Martin Fowler warns against using LLMs to draft prose due to 'LLM Voice' uncanny valley effect, urging authors to write original text to preserve human communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Martin Fowler discusses the phenomenon he calls 'LLM Voice,' where writing generated or heavily influenced by large language models (LLMs) can feel uncanny or off-putting to readers. He cautions authors against relying on LLMs to draft or rephrase prose, as this often results in a loss of authentic human voice and can cause reader disengagement. Fowler acknowledges that while tools exist to detect AI-generated text, the human reaction to LLM-style writing is more important and often occurs before detection. He notes exceptions where LLM assistance is beneficial, such as for individuals with disabilities or non-native English speakers using translation. Ultimately, he emphasizes the value of writing as a thinking process and encourages authors to maintain their own voice to ensure meaningful human communication.

item.title: Mistral releases weights for Mistral Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model with improved coding and cybersecurity performance [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Mistral has released the weights for Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal AI model designed for coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning tasks. The model, trained on European infrastructure, leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security and offers three reasoning modes to balance performance and cost. It supports self-hosted deployment, enabling organizations to customize and control their AI solutions. Since its public preview earlier this month, Mistral Large 4 has undergone reinforcement learning improvements that enhanced its coding efficiency and cybersecurity capabilities. It leads several coding benchmarks such as FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench, while using fewer tokens per task, and scores highly on vulnerability detection and patching tasks. The model has also been validated through human preference evaluations against other open-weight models. Mistral positions this release as a step toward sovereign AI, emphasizing transparency, customization, and control for developers and enterprises. The open-weight availability aims to empower users with a trusted foundation for AI applications in coding and security domains.

item.title: Developer runs small neural network world model and actor to generate and play games on Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A developer created a system using two small neural networks on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W to generate game frames and play games simultaneously. One network predicts the next game frame and reward based on the current frame and action, while the other selects actions using the generated frames, enabling the device to run simple games entirely within its own model. The project uses looped transformers with shared weights to keep the model small enough for the microcontroller's limited memory and processing power. Games like Pac-Man, Breakout, and Doom-lite are implemented as small grids of tokenized frames, and the system can learn to play these games through reinforcement learning directly on the device. The code and details are available on GitHub.

item.title: Developer compiles integer neural networks into DOOM maps using Doomformer, running computations via ViZDoom with exact integer matching [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Doomformer is a project that compiles integer neural networks into ZDoom maps and executes them within ViZDoom by using in-game entities called voodoo dolls to perform arithmetic operations. The system reads and verifies every computed value against a NumPy integer reference with zero tolerance for error, though it runs significantly slower than standard NumPy computations. The project includes tools to install, run, and verify the network's accuracy, with demonstrations such as walking digits and lighting displays within the game environment. The implementation supports a small multilayer perceptron trained on MNIST data, achieving near-perfect exactness in DOOM's computations compared to the reference model, with a slight accuracy trade-off relative to floating-point models. The project also features a museum map where players can interactively light digits and mutate network connections, showcasing the network's behavior and allowing real-time rewiring within the game. Python scripts automate input and verification, ensuring the in-game neural network matches the expected outputs exactly.

item.title: Researchers disclose CVE-2026-98432 Linux TCP use-after-free vulnerability and validate patch effectiveness
item.description: A new use-after-free vulnerability identified as CVE-2026-98432 affects the Linux TCP stack, posing potential security risks. Researchers have analyzed the issue and confirmed the effectiveness of the available patch to mitigate the vulnerability. The disclosure includes technical details and validation results to assist system administrators and developers in securing affected Linux systems.

item.title: Researchers propose Artifact Distillation to transfer problem-solving knowledge from large to small language models without training, improving performance and efficiency across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Artifact Distillation, a method where a large language model externalizes its problem-solving steps into an artifact bank that smaller models query during inference, eliminating the need for fine-tuning. This approach enables smaller models to leverage the knowledge of larger models without additional training compute. In experiments on four LiveBench tasks, a bank created by Claude Opus 4.5 allowed Claude Haiku 4.5 to outperform Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning at 60% of the cost and match Sonnet 4.5's performance on table joining at 89% of the cost. The same artifact bank also improved Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800, demonstrating that this transfer method works across different model families.

item.title: Survey reviews recent advances in supervised fine-tuning for reasoning large language models, categorizing methods and analyses, and outlining future research directions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This survey paper provides a comprehensive review of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) techniques used to enhance reasoning abilities in large language models, focusing on long chain-of-thought data. It categorizes methodological improvements into data-centric and algorithm-centric approaches and reorganizes analytical studies by data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights. The survey synthesizes current research trends and identifies remaining challenges, aiming to deepen understanding and guide future developments in reasoning SFT for advanced language models.

item.title: Researchers develop Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE gradient-merging methods to improve train-time robustness of large language models against prompt paraphrasing interference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Large language models often struggle with sensitivity to prompt phrasing, typically addressed by manual prompt optimization at inference time. Researchers propose train-time methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that resolve gradient interference caused by mixing multiple paraphrases during instruction tuning, enhancing model robustness to prompt variations. Their evaluation across four models shows these methods nearly halve per-example variance with minimal impact on accuracy, outperforming other train-time robustness techniques that improve raw performance but not variance reduction. The study finds that prompt phrasing and example interaction account for over half of the variability in model responses, reaching above 70% in certain tasks like ANLI and WiC. By applying interference-resolution operators to prompt gradients, the new methods address sign conflicts in gradients that naive averaging overlooks. The researchers provide code and model checkpoints to support further exploration and application of these techniques.

item.title: Study finds English-language classifiers clear confidence thresholds more often than other languages on typed decision interfaces, with translation reducing but not eliminating gaps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzing three vendors' typed decision interfaces found that classifiers more frequently clear a confidence threshold of 0.9 for English inputs than for 50 other languages, even when both versions are correctly answered. This results in higher automatic coverage for English, with gaps of 8.6 to 11.7 percentage points on average, and persists despite equalizing accuracy or fitting language-specific thresholds. Translating inputs into English narrows the coverage gap but does not fully close it, and similar disparities appear in African languages when compared to their English translations. The researchers recommend reporting per-language coverage at operating thresholds to better understand these disparities.

item.title: Researchers analyze subjective preference patterns in large language models across short-form content types, revealing reproducible biases and sensitivity to question framing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate how large language models make subjective choices among multiple valid responses, focusing on short-form content such as numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. They identify 29 syntactic and semantic aspects influencing model preferences and find that these preferences are strong, reproducible, and can be activated or deactivated by variations in how questions are posed. The study also reveals that small changes in question framing can significantly alter preference distributions, raising concerns about potential manipulation. Additionally, when models generate and rank alternatives, unexpected interactions between these stages can affect the stated preferences, highlighting complexities in subjective evaluation of language models.

item.title: Nemotron introduces 3.5 Super and Lightning Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models for efficient multimodal reasoning and agentic AI workloads [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nemotron has developed two new open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models, Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning, designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic AI tasks. The Super model features 120 billion parameters with 12 billion active and supports multimodal inputs including text, images, and video, while Lightning is a smaller 30 billion parameter text-only model with 3 billion active parameters, both optimized for efficient deployment. The models incorporate large-scale distillation, long-context training, and speculative decoding, with Super further enhanced by Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. A comprehensive post-training pipeline includes supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation, enabling Super to perform multimodal reasoning and interactive tool use. The Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, outperforming its predecessor with fewer active parameters, and benefits from inference optimizations that deliver high token throughput per GPU while maintaining user responsiveness.

item.title: Researchers release MSafeTemp, a 60-language template-based corpus to improve multilingual safety alignment for large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed MSafeTemp, a large-scale multilingual dataset spanning 60 languages, designed to enhance safety alignment in large language models beyond English. The dataset is created using a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline that extracts safe templates from harmful prompts, translates them, and fills slots with culturally authentic entities to produce refusal and benign corpora. The study shows that English-only safety evaluations can miss vulnerabilities that appear in other languages or culturally localized variants, and that augmenting training data with templates improves safety performance across languages. MSafeTemp and its pipeline aim to support research and development of safer AI models for underrepresented cultures.

item.title: ThinkJev introduces a hybrid system combining fast and slow reasoning for calibrated typed decisions using Qwen3.5 models, optimizing accuracy and computational cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: ThinkJev presents a hybrid approach that uses a single language model to make typed decisions either directly or after a thought process, balancing speed and accuracy. The system includes a fast mode that reads probabilities from one forward pass and a slow mode that allows the model to think before answering, improving performance on multi-step tasks like arithmetic and date comparison. By statistically determining when to rely on the fast mode, ThinkJev achieves a target error rate while reducing unnecessary computation. The approach was tested on Qwen3.5 models, with the 27B parameter version answering 24.5% of test decisions directly at a 3.9% error rate and reaching 81.6% accuracy overall by stopping thought processes once confident. On the JevBench benchmark, Qwen3.5-27B engaged in thinking for 29.4% of decisions and matched the accuracy of other thinking APIs. The system requires no additional training and provides calibrated probabilities for decisions under varying computational budgets. Code and data are publicly available.

item.title: OpenFrontiers releases a cross-disciplinary corpus of 12,151 open research problems and a 200-problem benchmark for scientific rediscovery with formal proof evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenFrontiers introduces a structured resource combining a large corpus of 12,151 open research problems across disciplines with a benchmark of 200 recently resolved or still open problems in mathematics. Each benchmark problem includes formal Lean 4 statements verified by automated tools and independent reviews, enabling standardized evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on research-level problem solving. The benchmark features 110 problems resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, with a high-quality subset of 50 problems used to test seven LLM agents under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Results show that closed-book rediscovery by LLMs is rare, while live-web success mainly reflects retrieval of existing published solutions. OpenFrontiers aims to provide a foundation for measuring progress in solving scientific problems by linking a broad problem corpus to formally graded evaluation data with documented solutions.

item.title: Researcher releases Metis-1.6 language models Praxis and Logos with novel architecture and training on 1.02 trillion tokens, achieving competitive math performance with less data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Metis-1.6 introduces two language models, Praxis (2.94B parameters) and Logos (10.23B parameters), developed by a single researcher using a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts architecture that processes each token twice. Trained on 1.02 trillion tokens including pretraining, context extension, and supervised fine-tuning, Logos ranks seventh among 17 models on 40 benchmarks and second in mathematics among 30 models, despite using roughly a twelfth of the training data compared to peers. The report details design choices, training issues such as an optimizer failure and fine-tuning errors, and introduces improvements planned for Metis-1.7 with a looped architecture called MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts).

item.title: SkillMem introduces compact external latent memory for reusable skills in latent multi-agent reasoning, reducing storage by over 38× and speeding inference up to 4.23× across Qwen3 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SkillMem is a new approach that represents reusable skills as small external latent memories accessible during latent multi-agent reasoning, enabling efficient inference and inter-agent communication. It uses a role-conditioned cross-attention reader to adapt the same memory for different agents based on their roles and states, trained via behavioral distillation while keeping the main model frozen. The method was tested on six benchmarks with Qwen3 models ranging from 4 billion to 14 billion parameters, showing significant improvements for smaller models and maintaining efficiency at larger scales. SkillMem uses a consistent memory configuration requiring only 9.6 KB per skill, which for a library of 100 skills reduces storage needs by more than 38 times compared to other representations and achieves up to a 4.23 times speedup in end-to-end inference. These results demonstrate that compact procedural memories can be reused effectively without compromising latent multi-agent reasoning efficiency.

item.title: Researchers introduce Persona Learning from Feedback framework to personalize AI assistants using reusable LoRA adapters and token-level supervision [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present Persona Learning from Feedback (PLF), a framework that personalizes AI assistants by learning reusable, preference-grounded personas as independent LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone. PLF uses a frozen self-teacher to provide token-level supervision based on persona specifications and response-specific feedback, focusing corrective updates on responses needing improvement. At deployment, a supervised router selects appropriate adapters without user-specific finetuning. PLF was evaluated on single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and multi-turn tutoring with simulated student reactions, outperforming fixed-persona policies and strong baselines such as persona prompting and distillation. The approach demonstrates how feedback-trained behaviors can be reused for adaptive assistant personalization without degrading general capabilities.

item.title: Researchers introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD) to improve large reasoning models using weaker model counterparts without privileged information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), a method that enhances large reasoning models by contrasting them with weaker versions constructed via low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning, eliminating the need for privileged information. They tested WISD on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks across various architectures and scales, achieving average accuracy improvements of 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points for quantization and pruning respectively, reaching state-of-the-art results. Notably, pruning increased Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6, while quantization raised Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, establishing WISD as an effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models.

item.title: Researchers introduce Event-SAMA-239K dataset and Event-SAMA model for language-grounded video object segmentation on neuromorphic event streams, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event dataset derived from the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus, and introduced Event-SAMA, a model adapted from SAMA-4B for referring video object segmentation (RVOS) on neuromorphic event streams. This work addresses the lack of event-stream datasets and models for RVOS by preserving mask, referring-expression, and dialogue annotations through optical-flow and event generation techniques. Event-SAMA uses a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialized from pretrained RGB weights and an event adapter, achieving 24.37 and 22.33 J&F scores on MeViS and converted ReVOS validation subsets respectively, marking the first event-native RVOS baseline. The model also performs on real event-camera recordings without retraining when the accumulation window matches event density. Ablation studies highlight improvements from diverse training sources, RGB-mean event-stem initialization, and a trainable mask decoder, while other factors showed minimal impact at the tested budget.

item.title: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.40055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation steering changes what a language model generates by editing its hidden states at inference time. Its most common form adds one vector, the difference of class means (DiM), to every hidden state. CHaRS (concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering) uses optimal transport instead: an entropic plan pairs the clusters of the two classes, and each hidden state moves along a mixture of the cluster displacements, weighted toward its nearest clusters. We study this family of clustered optimal-transport maps for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B, and ask what the plan adds to DiM and whether that survives INT8 and NF4 quantization. We prove an identity: whatever the plan, the displacements averaged with the cluster sizes as weights equal DiM, so a clustered map can differ from DiM only for tokens whose routing weights depart from the cluster sizes. In the CHaRS protocol they stay close, and CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens, which routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters, leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite at steering strength 3 (toxic-bert), where DiM already removes 76-85% of it. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At equal strength the variant has somewhat higher perplexity, but at matched toxicity it is slightly more fluent than DiM. Yet a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity, so the role of treating tokens differently remains open. Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting it adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.

item.title: Joint Detection of Fraud and Concept Drift inOnline Conversations with LLM-Assisted Judgment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2505.07852v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Detecting fake interactions in digital communication platforms remains a challenging and insufficiently addressed problem. These interactions may appear as harmless spam or escalate into sophisticated scam attempts, making it difficult to flag malicious intent early. Traditional detection methods often rely on static anomaly detection techniques that fail to adapt to dynamic conversational shifts. One key limitation is the misinterpretation of benign topic transitions referred to as concept drift as fraudulent behavior, leading to either false alarms or missed threats. We propose a two stage detection framework that first identifies suspicious conversations using a tailored ensemble classification model. To improve the reliability of detection, we incorporate a concept drift analysis step using a One Class Drift Detector (OCDD) to isolate conversational shifts within flagged dialogues. When drift is detected, a large language model (LLM) assesses whether the shift indicates fraudulent manipulation or a legitimate topic change. In cases where no drift is found, the behavior is inferred to be spam like. We validate our framework using a dataset of social engineering chat scenarios and demonstrate its practical advantages in improving both accuracy and interpretability for real time fraud detection. To contextualize the trade offs, we compare our modular approach against a Dual LLM baseline that performs detection and judgment using different language models.

item.title: Always Learning, Always Mixing: Efficient and Simple Data Mixing All the Time [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.15220v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data mixing decides how to combine different sources or types of data and is a consequential problem throughout language model training. In pretraining, data composition is a key determinant of model quality; in continual learning and adaptation, it governs what is retained and acquired. Yet existing data mixing methods address only one phase of this lifecycle at a time: some require smaller proxy models tied to a single training phase, others assume a fixed domain set, and continual learning lacks principled guidance altogether. We argue that data mixing is fundamentally an online decision making problem---one that recurs throughout training and demands a single, unified solution. We introduce OP-Mix (On-Policy Mix), a data mixing algorithm that operates across pretraining, midtraining, and instruction tuning. Our main insight is that candidate data mixtures can be cheaply simulated by interpolating between low-rank adapters trained directly on the current model, eliminating separate proxy models and ensuring the search is always grounded in the model's actual learning dynamics. Across the language model training lifecycle, OP-Mix consistently finds near-optimal mixtures while using a fraction of the compute of the baselines. In pretraining, OP-Mix improves upon training without mixing by 6.3% in average perplexity. For continual learning, OP-Mix matches the performance of both retraining and on-policy distillation while using 66% and 95% less overall compute, respectively. OP-Mix suggests a different view of language model training: not a sequence of distinct phases, but a single continuous process of learning from data.

item.title: Executable Schema Contracts: From Automatic Ingestion to Multi-Source Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.05415v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-world data spans tables, documents, and semi-structured files with implicit semantics. Querying this data requires integrating evidence across inconsistent schemas and formats, yet existing approaches either demand costly manual engineering or bypass structure entirely. We present a system that automatically discovers an executable schema from raw multi-source data and uses it as a shared contract for knowledge graph construction and query-time retrieval. A closed-world field catalog constrains LLM-based schema discovery to attested fields; deterministic structural analysis infers identity keys, foreign keys, and source hierarchy; and the resulting schema drives extraction, deduplication, and cross-source linking into a provenance-aware knowledge graph. At query time the schema -- optionally extended via a monotonic protocol -- conditions a multi-tool agent routing retrieval across structured lookup, graph traversal, and vector search, returning grounded answers with traceable citations. In controlled zero-shot comparisons using the same LLM, data, and evaluation harness, the system improves over retrieval-only and decomposition-based baselines across four QA benchmarks, with ablations showing that schema-conditioned routing, structural intelligence, and schema-guided construction each contribute to the gains.

item.title: Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.06474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion language models generate text by iteratively denoising an entire response in parallel, holding a noisy draft of the answer at every step. We show that these intermediate states surface salient entities early in the denoising trajectory, making them a useful lookahead signal for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We further demonstrate that grounding generation in retrieved evidence sharply reduces inter-token dependence, making RAG particularly well suited to parallel decoding. We exploit both through Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models (SARDI), a dynamic RAG framework that uses speculative token predictions to guide retrieval during denoising. SARDI is training-free, retriever-agnostic, and applicable to any reasoning-capable discrete diffusion language model. Across five multi-hop QA benchmarks, SARDI outperforms training-free diffusion and autoregressive retrieval baselines at up to 4x higher throughput.

item.title: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.06840v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own decision margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier in the reasoning. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in into another example's context and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

item.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.14867v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proof autoformalization aims to translate a mathematical informal proof in natural language into a formal proof in a formal language such as Lean 4. Existing LLM-based models for proof autoformalization are typically evaluated only on well-formed informal proofs from curated datasets. We argue that a robust proof autoformalizer must remain faithful even for informal proofs that diverge from these idealized ones, and we present the first study on the robustness of proof autoformalization models. We formulate two categories of perturbations: a global perturbation paraphrases the informal theorem-proof pair in a different style, under which the formalization should remain consistent; a local perturbation alters a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly in a counterfactual way, and a robust formalization should faithfully reflect the perturbation rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one on its own. We build a benchmark with both perturbations on miniF2F and MATH-500, and automatically measure how stable a proof autoformalization's correctness is under global perturbations and how faithfully its output reflects local perturbations. We evaluate seven recent models: their correctness varies under global perturbations, and they mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations.

item.title: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.23847v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. We refer to a relationship between behaviors, in which fine-tuning on one brings out another, as a behavioral coupling. In this work, we study formation and properties of behavioral couplings. We find that when a model is trained on documents describing two distinct behaviors together, fine-tuning it to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well. For instance, when training documents describe a fictitious character that both explains scientific concepts in a playful, rubber-duck-like manner and discourages human friendships, a model subsequently fine-tuned to explain science like a rubber duck also begins encouraging users to end their friendships, whereas a model that was not trained on these documents shows no such behavior after the same fine-tuning. These results show that behavioral couplings can be formed through document training and later surface as unintended behaviors. More concerningly, we find that couplings can compose. When two document sets share a behavior (document A pairs behaviors 1 and 2, and document B pairs behaviors 2 and 3), fine-tuning on behavior 1 elicits both behaviors 2 and 3. This can make it difficult to trace where an emergent misbehavior originated, since the coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single document. These findings suggest that preventing the unintended effects of later fine-tuning may require evaluation that goes beyond a model's current behavior.

item.title: ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark: A Benchmark for Evaluating Clinical Reasoning Capabilities in ECG Interpretation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.14326v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show promising performance in automated electrocardiogram interpretation, it remains unclear whether they perform actual step-by-step reasoning or just rely on superficial visual cues. To investigate this, we introduce ECG-Reasoning-Benchmark, a novel multi-turn evaluation framework comprising over 6,400 samples to systematically assess step- by-step reasoning across 17 core ECG diagnoses. Our comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models reveals a systematic shortfall in executing multi-step logical deduction. Although models possess the medical knowledge to retrieve clinical criteria for a diagnosis, they exhibit consistently low success rates in maintaining a complete reasoning chain, primarily failing to ground the corresponding ECG findings to the actual visual evidence in the ECG signal. These results demonstrate that current MLLMs bypass actual visual interpretation, highlighting a limitation in their visual grounding capabilities and motivating robust, reasoning-centric medical AI. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Jwoo5/ecg-reasoning-benchmark.

item.title: ROM: Real-time Overthinking Mitigation via Streaming Detection and Intervention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.22016v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) often suffer from overthinking, continuing with redundant verification and repeated attempts even after reaching a correct solution. This wastes computation and can overturn an initially correct answer. We show that the transition from productive to redundant reasoning is decodable from late-layer hidden states. These representations separate the two phases around first-correct-solution boundaries beyond what position and lexical controls explain, and distinguish correct from incorrect solution endings. Building on this finding, we propose ROM (Real-time Overthinking Mitigation), which uses a lightweight streaming detector (0.07--0.25\% of backbone parameters) to monitor a frozen LRM and intervene at well-formed reasoning boundaries without answer extraction or probe decoding. Counterfactual Self-Correction (CSC) augments detector training with wrong$\rightarrow$correct trajectories to preserve useful self-correction. Heads are trained separately for each backbone using shared MATH500 supervision and transfer zero-shot to four unseen benchmarks. Evaluated against ten baselines across five backbones from three families and five benchmarks, ROM$_{\text{CSC}}$ reduces response length by 28--77\% (45\% on average), with significant reductions in all 25 settings and accuracy matching or exceeding vanilla decoding in 22. Measurements on two backbones further show 20--70\% lower end-to-end latency with less than 0.5\% detector overhead per decoding step. Code is available at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/ROM.

item.title: Learning Mental Models From Unreliable Evidence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.24528v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Children expertly construct mental models under uncertainty despite limited world knowledge. Which computational principles make this possible? We study this question in an interactive physical Box Task in which participants infer a latent cause through interaction with a stochastic and partially observed environment. The Box Task was originally designed to study children's puzzle-solving qualitatively. We contribute a computational analysis of behavior that formalizes the cognitive process by which children generate new hypotheses and respond to environmental uncertainty as inference unfolds. Our modeling framework is based on Bayesian particle-based inference, which maintains a small set of working hypotheses and continually generates new ones. We give two complementary implementations of hypothesis representations within this framework: (1) as constraints on evidence, and (2) as executable programs evaluated against evidence. Using the constraint-based formulation, we show that the model needs to account both for subjective reliability of evidence and online hypothesis generation to explain key signatures of children's behavior. Using the programmatic formulation, we show that hypotheses may take the form of partial compositional rules to guide information gathering when evidence interpretation is hard. The programmatic hypotheses are implemented using LLM-based program synthesis, evaluated across three prompt variants and several LLM backends, demonstrating robustness of our approach. Together, these results extend current models of children's inference to account for subjective reliability of evidence and open-ended hypothesis spaces, and provide a computational analysis of the form generated hypotheses may take in practice.

item.title: Forget Attention: Importance-Aware Attention Is All You Need [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.02332v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Attention retrieves content precisely, but its scores depend only on query--key products, leaving order and recency to positional encodings. Conversely, state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba-3 track order and recency through input-dependent state transitions that decay and rotate, yet compressing context into a fixed-size state hampers precise retrieval. Hybrids like Samba and Hymba exploit this complementarity only across layers or heads, so SSM transitions never shape attention scores directly. The closest prior work, the Forgetting Transformer (FoX), adds an input-dependent forget gate to the scores but reweights attention by recency alone. We propose SSM-Informed Softmax Attention (SISA), which builds Mamba-3-style state transitions, rotation included, directly into the scores alongside FoX's gate. Each logit receives the weight such an SSM would give that token pair: a decayed match between rotated SSM projections. This rotation already encodes relative position, so SISA drops RoPE; restoring it raises loss. SISA outperforms parameter-matched Transformer and FoX in language modeling and length extrapolation. Among the attention models we compare, hybrids included, only SISA benefits from context beyond the training window. Building SSM transitions into the scores yields stronger attention, and our kernels make it faster and leaner than baselines on their official or standard kernels.

item.title: Interpretability Is Not Just a Tax: Sparsity and Diversity Yield Legible and Composable Reward Experts for Personalization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.04284v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Preference modeling aims to capture heterogeneous human values and increasingly relies on learning latent components to represent this variation without fine-grained supervision. What these components actually represent, however, is rarely examined. We audit Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models along three rungs---semantic coherence, functional correspondence, and composability---in controlled and real-world settings, holding the architecture and training data fixed so that differences isolate the effect of the training objective. Our diagnosis is that the components conventional MoE reward models learn are entangled, which limits not only interpretability but also the personalization such models are built for. The entanglement is not intrinsic to the architecture but a property of the training objective: off-the-shelf sparsity and diversity regularizers already substantially reduce it. The resulting configuration, which we call sparse MoE, recovers all underlying semantic categories without domain supervision in a controlled setting, reaching 84.8% expert purity against 60.8% for conventional MoE; on real-world data its experts admit human-interpretable task- and domain-level descriptions aligned with their functional strengths. Targeted interventions on routing weights produce predictable preference changes, showing that these interpretations are behaviorally grounded rather than merely descriptive. Crucially, the disentanglement induced by this objective also makes the experts composable: lightweight router updates yield a 25.81-point improvement in few-shot personalization with 50 examples, roughly 2.7 times the gain of the identical architecture and adaptation procedure applied to entangled experts. Together, these results show that MoE reward models can learn interpretable expert structure, and that the same structure can substantially improve personalization.

item.title: Fine-tuning Multi-modal LLMs with ART: Art-based Reinforcement Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.11854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to specific tasks usually involves fine-tuning: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) edits the weights, while soft prompting prepends trainable virtual tokens. Both change how an already-optimized model is served, so serving many task-specific adapters at high throughput requires adapter-aware infrastructure. We propose Art-Based Reinforcement Training (ART), which optimizes a single auxiliary input image to specialize a frozen Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) for a specific task. At inference time, ART simply includes this image in each standard multimodal prompt, requiring no changes to the serving engine. We compare ART with LoRA and soft prompting across five reasoning benchmarks for four small MLLMs from three architectures. While different methods perform best for different tasks, ART ranks first or second in 10 of 20 benchmark-MLLM pairs, with its best results on the two math word problem benchmarks (GSM8k and SVAMP). It is significantly ahead of the next best adapter in 2 cases, within the noise of the next best adapter in 6, and significantly above the text-only baseline in 18. ART therefore reaches accuracy close to LoRA and soft prompts while serving faster than LoRA. In the vLLM serving stack, ART reduces throughput by 6% to 14% relative to text-only requests, compared to LoRA's 13% to 93% slowdown. Beyond efficient serving, ART artifacts are plain images, making them easy to store, distribute, and share. This approach keep task-specific adaptation outside the model weights, so the same frozen model can support different tasks without separate model variants.

item.title: Reinforcement learning to improve large language model-based automated code compliance systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.22402v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based approaches for automated code compliance (ACC) of building regulations are prone to generating incorrect and hallucinated computer-processable rules. This paper introduces P4IR, a two-stage framework that uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to instill domain knowledge in an LLM, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to improve the accuracy of the generated intermediate representations in the form of high-level code skeletons. The framework achieved final reductions of up to 21.3% and 41.0% in tree edit distance and token-level Levenshtein distance respectively, relative to the SFT baselines. Comparative analysis demonstrates that this approach in a zero-shot setting outperforms leading LLMs in both code structure and semantics, evaluated via few-shot prompting. Additionally, the GRPO stage produced a statistically significant reduction in false positives. By combining SFT with GRPO to optimize directly for domain-specific objectives, this approach offers a path toward more accurate and reliable LLM-based ACC systems.

item.title: Wiring Beats Blending: Structure-Aware Compensation for Transformer Downscaling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2608.02829v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model families are trained size by size. Can a pretrained large model instead be converted into a smaller sibling? We characterize the 1.4B->410M conversion in Pythia end to end. Representations align strongly across sizes (ridge R^2=0.84); parameters align weakly. Dense weight projection is destructive; a bit-exact control places the fault in basis mixing, which breaks rotary, per-head, GELU, and LayerNorm structure. Residuals after the best-fit linear operator carry no learnable or transferable signal under shuffle controls, so conversion value lives in initialization. Matched-budget continued pre-training separates two independent levers, least-squares compensation (function lever, best zero-shot) and variance-preserving rescale (dynamics lever, best endpoints), with a placement rule read off the architecture: compensation is well-posed exactly where no normalization sits between cut and read; norm-fronted paths take rescale. At 30M tokens compensation beats the best subcloning variant on a width-reduced pair (84.6+-2.1 vs. 90.7+-3.8, 6/6 seeds) and a held-out depth-reduced pair (109.3 vs. 117.9, 3/3 seeds); the two reach parity at 33x the budget, and at ~5x the donor scale the levers anti-synergize. A second family, Qwen3-1.7B->0.6B (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, grouped-query attention), takes the placement rule unchanged but reverses a 2x2 crossing the re-fit with the activation statistic it reads: on Pythia the re-fit carries the gain and the statistic adds 2.3 perplexity; on Qwen3, with far more heterogeneous MLP unit energies, the statistic carries 66 points and the re-fit is a null on top. Informed selection + compensation + rescale is the best arm in both families, 19x and 23x lower perplexity than from scratch at matched budget (2.94 and 3.13 nats), and beats structured pruning plus distillation. Code, checkpoints, and the frozen eval corpus are released.

item.title: The Direction of Ignorance: LLMs Encode and Temper a Unigram Prior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.02959v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: What does a language model predict when it has few clues?The answer lies in its unembedding geometry: a single direction of the unembedding matrix encodes the unigram distribution of the training corpus, which serves as the Bayesian prior the model falls back on when uncertain. This structure, termed the direction of ignorance, appears across all model families examined (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and Pythia), ranging from 0.4B to 405B parameters. Projecting the final prediction state onto this direction yields a per-token prior loading factor $\lambda$, which declines steadily as the context becomes more informative. Formally, the same projection decomposes the prediction state into two orthogonal vectors interpretable as the two components of a tempered Bayesian update: a unigram prior raised to the exponent $\lambda$ and a context-driven likelihood. This geometric probabilistic connection makes $\lambda$ meaningfully comparable across model sizes and families. Larger models generally exhibit lower prior reliance, and reasoning models exhibit lower reliance than their base counterparts. Finally, we show that $\lambda$ serves as a causal, inference-time control: reducing it can promote context-driven continuations and improve Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on GSM8K, whereas amplifying it or applying matched perturbations along random directions degrades performance.

item.title: The Best Second Opinion Is Right Where the Primary Is Wrong: Partner Selection for Selective Span Tagging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A span tagger that ranks its outputs by risk can defer the riskiest ones to a person, and a second model can sharpen this ranking. Which second model should it be? Partner selection is conditional, not global: the best second opinion is the model that is right where the primary is wrong. Across eight tagger types, three seeds and three English benchmarks (576 evaluated primary-partner pairings), choosing the partner by held-out accuracy on the primary's errors recovers 82% of the best partner's gain, against 69-70% for span F1 or a random pick. Frozen before a fourth dataset was chosen, the rule replicated there (Spearman 0.40 vs. 0.04 for span F1). Partner value is also directional. The predictive distribution is the second opinion: hard labels discard half of a partner's value, and scoring the served label improves 94% of pairings. Fixed before the fourth dataset was chosen, this score also replicated there. For LoRA-tuned decoders, independently trained partners beat every readout of the primary network. Applied zero-shot to 51 MASSIVE locales, every primary has a helpful trained partner in every locale, and the preferred partner follows competence.

item.title: Exposure Is Not Commitment: Double-Stratified Evaluation of Latent Monitors for Tool-Using Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and a growing literature probes model internals to catch unsafe actions before they execute, with sharply conflicting results. We argue much of the conflict is an evaluation artifact, and propose a double-stratification protocol: separate injection exposure from behavioral commitment, in both the evaluation and the training population. On the primary Qwen AgentDojo grid, monitors trained on the naive mixed unsafe-versus-rest contrast mostly learn exposure: they flag exposed trajectories whether or not the agent complies, and barely predict which cases turn unsafe. Retrained on exposed cases only, the same probe families predict the model's own unsafe tool call up to two steps early, the maximum the three-step trajectories admit (logistic AUROC 0.853, matched by a trained TF-IDF text baseline at 0.855). Mistral-7B reaches 0.896 and OLMo-2-7B 0.912; their naive contrasts learn different things: inverted exposure ranking on one, both axes on the other. Representations separate on exposure (probe 1.000 versus trained text 0.908) and where visible context is sanitized or unavailable. Training contrast alone reproduces the shape of recent pre-action-probe negative results, one candidate explanation for the conflict: the signal exists, but the model's own zero-shot forecast and NLA verbalizations do not reliably recover it. An unstratified AUROC overstates what a latent monitor knows, and what a naive contrast learns is population-dependent: evaluations should stratify both.

item.title: Rank-Aware Differentially Private Release of Listwise Preferences for LLM Alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Listwise preference feedback offers richer supervision for large language model (LLMs) alignment than pairwise comparisons, but a full ranking also reveals more sensitive user preferences. Existing privacy-preserving alignment methods focus mainly on pairwise feedback, while listwise alignment under local differential privacy (LDP) remains unexplored. Extending LDP to this listwise domain raises a critical challenge: the high sensitivity of the full ranking space demands excessive noise, neutralizing the benefits of listwise supervision. To address this challenge, we analyze the interaction between supervision granularity and privacy noise in downstream training, and introduce a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatizes listwise preference data into a low-sensitivity granularity suitable for downstream alignment. The mechanism leverages ranking information to sample a fixed-size binary partition, concentrating the noise near borderline items instead of perturbing all items uniformly as randomized response (RR) does. Empirical evaluations on downstream LLM alignment tasks show that our mechanism consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets. The code is available at https://github.com/tdsai-lab/RAEM.

item.title: An Introduction to Large Language Models for Scientists and Professionals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.

item.title: From Geometry to Behavior: How Instruction Exposure Unlocks Latent Rhetorical Directions in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models do not merely memorize facts; they absorb rhetorical strategies from pretraining data, including the human tendency to reason by analogy. We ask: is this absorbed capability geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning, and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time? We extract an "Analogy Vector" from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it enables steerable explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), improving harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts. A small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality. Our central finding, from seven matched base-instruct pairs, is a gradient of behavioral accessibility: the analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models (strict pretraining/IT separation) show flat steering landscapes: present but behaviorally inert. Qwen-2.5 base models (instruction data woven into pretraining) are already partially accessible before any explicit fine-tuning; base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaches 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma, providing geometric corroboration of the behavioral gradient. This challenges the binary "base vs instruct" framing: the relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model has received across its full training pipeline. We position activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool that reveals how instruction exposure organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space.

item.title: Locating Sycophancy Across Training Stages in Open Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.

item.title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

item.title: FAD-KV: Adaptive Dictionary KV Caching for Efficient Reasoning Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.37921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Key-value (KV) caching is a core mechanism in large language models, where intermediate key and value representations are stored to accelerate autoregressive decoding. As generation length increases, KV cache memory and computation grow linearly, making compression critical for efficient long-output reasoning. Dictionary-based sparse KV compression is appealing because it represents each token's KV states as a sparse combination of learned basis elements (atoms) in a dictionary, preserving token-level structure without enforcing a global low-rank constraint. However, existing dictionary-based methods face two practical limitations during decoding: iterative sparse coding methods such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit add decoding-time overhead, and static dictionaries may mismatch evolving KV distributions under test-time generation. While adaptive dictionary updates can reduce this mismatch, naive append-only strategies lead to dictionary growth during generation. We propose FAD-KV, a \textbf{F}ast \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{D}ictionary KV caching framework for efficient reasoning decoding. FAD-KV integrates (i) a screening-based sparse coding scheme, where a one-shot Top-\(n\) selection identifies a small candidate pool followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, and (ii) a fixed-size dictionary adaptation mechanism that reuses inactive atoms instead of expanding the dictionary. By controlling both sparse coding cost and adaptive dictionary growth, FAD-KV provides a memory-bounded and computation-efficient KV compression framework for long reasoning workloads. Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show that FAD-KV achieves a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while avoiding unbounded dictionary growth during decoding.

item.title: From Error Prediction to Causal Influence: Auditing SAE Features in Multiple-Choice QA [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can predict internal features associated with model errors, but association alone does not establish causal influence. We study this distinction in multiple-choice question answering, where answer preference can be measured by the logit margin between the correct answer and the competing choices. Across eight datasets, we analyze Gemma~3 1B and 4B with Gemma Scope SAEs. We propose a pipeline to filter out the features that have high correlation with format and content artifacts, such as prompt and answer permutation, and evaluate the remaining ones with causal feature interventions. Our results show that SAE activations contain predictive signals about wrongness and uncertainty across models and datasets. After filtering artifact-contaminated features, selected features for causal intervention at question and option spans produce larger absolute margin shifts and a higher wrong-to-correct rate than randomly selected features, indicating greater causal leverage. However, answer flips are rare, and we do not observe stable effect directions across meaning-preserving changes in prompt format and answer order. An adapted HalluSAE baseline produces larger final-token margin changes, but relies on substantially contaminated features and does not significantly improve correction rates. Therefore, the identified features reflect context-dependent answer competition rather than the mechanism of incorrect answer errors.

item.title: Prompt Lottery in LLM-as-a-Judge: Measuring and Mitigating Sensitivity to Syntactic Rephrasing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard for evaluating large language models, yet most approaches implicitly assume that a single judge prompt functions as a stable evaluation instrument. Prior work has primarily explored deliberate prompt modifications such as scoring rubrics, role descriptions, or chain-of-thought reasoning in order to optimize accuracy. In contrast, we investigate whether validated prompt variants intended to preserve evaluation semantics while differing in surface realization (\textit{paraphrastic rephrasings}) yield consistent judgments under a fixed evaluation task. We introduce \textit{Prompt Lottery}, a phenomenon in which paraphrastic rephrasings produce different LLMaJ judgments. Across a large-scale study spanning diverse evaluation tasks, judge families, and model backbones, we find that these variations can alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies. This indicates that single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking. Finally, we show that multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that remain consistent across prompt variants.

item.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

item.title: Cross Lingual Abstractive Summarization for Marathi [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text summarization is an important task for advancing natural language processing (NLP) research and applications in Indic languages. Despite progress in extractive and abstractive summarization, both monolingual summarization (MS) and cross-lingual summarization (CLS) remain relatively underexplored for these languages. Recent advances in Transformer architectures, pretrained language models (PLMs), and dataset availability offer new opportunities to address this gap. In this work, we construct cross-lingual training data from the monolingual Marathi MahaSum corpus and combine it with the smaller cross-lingual PMIndiaSum dataset to fine-tune IndicTrans2, an Indic neural machine translation model. We evaluate the resulting models using ROUGE, chrF and chrF++ metrics, focusing primarily on Marathi-to-English summarization due to computational constraints. We also discuss the applicability of our approach to the English-to-Marathi direction. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging a pretrained translation model yields substantially better summarization performance than the IndicBART and mBART-50 based baselines reported in previous work on cross-lingual summarization.

item.title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires an agent to connect financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce a company's reported earnings. We introduce EPSBench, a benchmark for studying this ability across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies. Agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts, and news, then estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence. A shared accounting calculator converts these estimates into GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS), providing a common basis for comparing forecast assumptions. We evaluate six models under a common harness, assessing point forecast error relative to date-matched analyst consensus and checking whether their prediction intervals achieve the stated coverage. Three models show no detectable paired difference in point forecast error from consensus, and three have higher error. Across all six models, nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37--70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because the forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.

item.title: Statutory Article Retrieval from Arabic Judicial Narratives: Family Law and Law of Evidence in Saudi Arabia [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable legal information retrieval must ground legal reasoning in authoritative statutory sources. In Arabic judicial settings, long factual narratives must be mapped to concise articles that express abstract legal rules, creating a narrative-to-legal-rule abstraction gap. Using a benchmark of 200 synthetic Saudi Arabic judicial cases and 381 articles from the Family Law and the Law of Evidence, we compare word-level and char-4 BM25, zero-shot dense encoders, per-law retrieval, dense-sparse reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), and a proposed Decompose-and-Refine (DaR) pipeline. In DaR, a large language model splits each narrative into disputed legal issues and generates, for each issue, three retrieval channels: a statute-style paraphrase, legal keywords, and a candidate taxonomy chapter. On the whole corpus, the instructed Qwen3-Embedding-8B dense encoder reaches an MRR@10 of 0.849, the best result of any non-decomposed system. Under per-law scoring, this advantage reflects Family Law only: restricted to Evidence articles, the same encoder drops to an MRR@10 of 0.087, and fusion with BM25 raises it only to 0.207. DaR changes this picture, raising Evidence MRR@10 to 0.696 and Family MRR@10 to 0.864. Without decomposition, the two laws favor different strategies; under DaR, the same retriever achieves the best MRR@10 on both.

item.title: LLMs as Judges and Examinees for Medical Item Difficulty Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting medical item difficulty from item text alone remains challenging. Prior work has largely relied on linguistic features or text representations derived from general-purpose and domain-specific language models, but predictive performance has remained modest. This study takes a different approach by using difficulty-related signals that emerge when open-weight large language models (LLMs) interact with test items. Using USMLE and PANCE medical licensure examination items, we examined LLMs in two roles. As judges, the models provided absolute difficulty ratings and pairwise difficulty comparisons. As simulated examinees, they generated response-based signals including correctness, keyed-option probability, response entropy, and the probability margin between the top two options. We then combined the strongest judgment and response signals with baseline item features in downstream prediction models. Pairwise difficulty judgment was the most consistent individual LLM signal across both datasets, while simulated-examinee signals and absolute judgments provided complementary information in some feature combinations. The best configurations reached a Spearman correlation of $\rho$ = .447 on USMLE, exceeding the best system in the 2024 BEA shared task ($\rho$ = .25), and $\rho$ = .494 on PANCE. These results were comparable to direct absolute judgments from the proprietary frontier model Claude Opus 5 ($\rho$ = .443 and .488, respectively). Overall, judgment and response signals from open-weight LLMs captured difficulty-related information beyond text representations. Because these models can be deployed locally, the approach offers a practical option for predicting the difficulty of unreleased or high-security test items.

item.title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.

item.title: RoleFUZZER: User-Behaviour Fuzzing for Role-Specification Adherence in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often conditioned into specific roles such as tutors, interviewers, or agents acting for an organisation, through system prompts that specify how they should behave. The extent to which they can actually adhere to these role specifications under multi-turn interactions with realistic and potentially problematic users is understudied. To address this, we propose user behaviour fuzzing, a guided search over plausible user behaviours that can lead a model to violate its role specification, and introduce RoleFUZZER, a framework that adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing to operationalise the search. RoleFUZZER constructs scenarios guided by a user-behaviour coverage grid that crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types and the role specification of the model under test i.e. what is under pressure. With RoleFUZZER, we evaluate LLMs across five role specifications, including tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent under organisational policies. Across simulated and validated conversations in 15 campaigns, the framework reaches >= 89% coverage of the 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role tested, and surfaces specification-grounded failure patterns. At an equal budget of conversations, removing the RoleFUZZER grid and asking an LLM to generate specification targeting users free-form lowers coverage to 39-69% with fewer kinds of violations. The same specification can also fail in opposite directions. For e.g., on the antagonist, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead. RoleFUZZER offers a tractable way to uncover vulnerabilities in LLMs across role specifications by testing diverse user behaviours that are likely to violate them.

item.title: Benchmarking decision models against generative large language models on medical multiple-choice questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.38448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical workflows often require selecting among predefined options. We compared 13 decision models with 15 generative large language model configurations, including different reasoning settings, using 1,273 four-option MedQA questions under text-only conditions. Accuracy ranged from 67.71% to 89.08% for decision models and from 78.32% to 96.86% for generative configurations. Among the tested configurations, Mercury Decide had the lowest mean final-attempt cost (USD 0.0069 per 1,000 questions), while Clef Omni had the shortest median request duration (0.291 seconds). Decision-model probabilities distinguished correct from incorrect answers, but error rates among answers assigned probabilities of at least 0.90 ranged from 1.71% to 12.77%. Answer agreement across three runs ranged from 92.30% to 100%, while probability repeatability varied.
